e.t: This word means “message”—something communicated or delivered for others to hear. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in 1 John, so its basic sense is focused and clear rather than broad or varied. The word identifies the content being conveyed, without by itself explaining whether that message is encouraging, instructive, or corrective. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but the central idea remains a communicated message.

This word means a “fish-hook” or “fishhook,” referring to the small hooked tool used to catch a fish. It is a concrete noun rather than a description of a person or an abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 17:27. The word’s basic meaning is therefore specific and practical: a hook used in fishing. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but the word itself names the fishing implement.

This word describes someone who is “motherless,” or “without a mother.” It focuses on the absence of a mother in relation to a person, rather than describing an action or quality such as strength or weakness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 7:3. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is a person considered without a mother.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Subjunctive, third, Plural

e.t: This word means “to invite in reciprocation” or “to invite in return.” It describes responding to another person’s invitation by inviting that person back, rather than extending an invitation only in one direction. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 14:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic idea is a reciprocal invitation or returned hospitality.

Antipas is a personal name. It does not function as a description or action word; it identifies someone by name. In the Greek New Testament, Antipas occurs once, in Revelation 2:13. Because the available wording gives only the name itself and not a definition beyond “Antipas,” its lexical meaning is simply the person’s name, while the surrounding verse supplies any further significance. This is a Greek New Testament name, not a general term used throughout Scripture.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “appropriately” or “worthily,” describing conduct that fits the person, calling, or standard being spoken about. It functions as an adverb, showing how someone should act rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, consistently pointing to behavior that suitably reflects what is valued or expected. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Arimathea is the name of a place. It is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times, in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Each occurrence identifies Arimathea in connection with Joseph, who is called Joseph of Arimathea. The name therefore functions as a geographical designation identifying Joseph’s home or place of origin, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular details. The Greek New Testament occurrences are Matthew 27:57, Mark 15:43, Luke 23:51, and John 19:38.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, first, Plural

e.t: This word means “be unsettled” or “to be homeless,” describing a person without stable security or a settled dwelling. It expresses a condition of wandering or lacking a permanent place rather than a chosen, comfortable way of life. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 4:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is living without settled shelter or stability.

This word means “torturer,” referring to a person who inflicts suffering as punishment or coercion. It is a noun naming such an individual, rather than describing the act itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 18:34. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word’s central sense is a person who tortures or subjects someone to harsh treatment.

Golgotha is the name of the place where Jesus was taken for crucifixion. It is a proper place name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: Matthew 27:33, Mark 15:22, and John 19:17. Each occurrence is rendered “Golgotha,” preserving the name rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive term. The exact significance of the place in any one passage is understood from that passage’s surrounding account.

This word expresses movement or connection “through” something, and it can also identify the reason “because of” which something happens. It therefore links an action, event, or result with either its means, passage, or cause. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 667 times, so its precise English wording depends on how it functions in each sentence. Its central idea remains a connection made through something or on account of something.

“Reformation” describes a change that brings about “a new order” or “reform,” rather than merely a minor adjustment. It can refer to the establishment of a different or improved arrangement. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs twice: in Acts 24:2 and Hebrews 9:10. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, which are not included here.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to invite” or “to invite into,” describing the action of asking someone to come in or join others. It functions as a verb, focusing on the act of extending such an invitation rather than on the person invited or the place entered. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 10:23. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its full sentence.

This word means “light,” describing something that is not heavy or burdensome. It can refer to the weight or difficulty of something, rather than to brightness. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, including language about a burden and about affliction being comparatively light. Its exact force in either verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains something easy to carry or relatively light in weight or hardship.

This word means “godliness” or “piety”: reverence toward God expressed as a devoted way of life. It describes a person’s serious orientation toward God rather than merely an outward religious appearance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 15 times, with many uses in 1 Timothy and several in 2 Peter. Its precise emphasis in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a life marked by genuine devotion to God.

This word refers to “a settled habit” or to “customs”—patterns of behavior that have become established and familiar. It can describe a personal practice or the customary ways shared by a community. The emphasis is on what people regularly follow, rather than on a single, passing action. In the Greek New Testament, the word occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 15:33. Its precise force there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is an established habit or customary practice.

This word means “religion,” referring to the practice or expression of worship. It is a noun that identifies a recognized religious life or devotion rather than a single action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Acts, Colossians, and James. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains religion or religious practice.

This word means “priesthood.” It refers to the priestly group or priestly status being spoken of, rather than to one individual priest. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, and both occurrences are in 1 Peter chapter 2. Its normal lexical force is a collective term connected with priests, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how it is being applied. It is rendered “priesthood” in both passages.

me: Verb, Present, Middle, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “reflecting” or “to reflect.” It describes an active process in which something is reflected, like an image in a mirror. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 3:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is the act of reflecting.

This Greek New Testament word means “to be consumed by fire” or “to burn.” It describes something undergoing burning or being overtaken by fire, functioning as an action rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in 2 Peter 3, where its precise force is understood from the surrounding passage. Its central idea remains the same: being burned or consumed by fire.

This word means “money exchanger” or “moneychanger”—a person who exchanges one kind of currency for another. It is a noun referring to people involved in handling or changing money, rather than to money itself. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 21:12, Mark 11:15, and John 2:15. Its central meaning remains the person who exchanges money, while the exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “marrow,” the soft substance found inside bones. It is a concrete bodily term, naming an inner part of the skeleton rather than an emotion, action, or abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 4:12. The word’s basic meaning remains simple and specific: the material within a bone. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical sense itself is “marrow.”

This word means “law,” referring to an established body of commands or instruction. It is a noun used to name law rather than to describe an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 9:4, so its normal meaning is represented by that single occurrence. The surrounding passage is needed to understand the particular emphasis in that verse, but the word itself points plainly to law as an authoritative standard or instruction.

This word refers to a “house servant” or “slave”—a person serving within a household under another’s authority. It identifies someone whose role is defined by service to a household master, rather than by independent status. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, each in a different verse. Its exact emphasis in any particular passage depends on how the surrounding sentence describes the servant’s relationship and responsibilities.

e.t: This word means “to give a name” or “to name.” It describes the act of assigning, declaring, or identifying someone or something by name. In the Greek New Testament, it is used 10 times, covering occasions where people are named or a name is formally given. Its basic sense remains focused on naming rather than on describing the person’s character, role, or significance; those details must come from the surrounding passage.

This word means “encouragement”: words or help that strengthen, comfort, or urge people onward. In the Greek New Testament, it refers to something given to believers for their benefit, including instruction that builds them up and strengthens their resolve. It occurs 29 times across 28 New Testament verses, showing a recurring concern for people to receive support and spiritual strengthening. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to strip off,” describing the removal of something from a person or object. It points to taking away an outer covering, garment, or attached item rather than merely moving it aside. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 16:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the act of stripping something away.

“Spiritual” describes what belongs to, comes from, or relates to the spirit rather than merely to ordinary physical life. In the New Testament, this adjective can describe people, nourishment, gifts, understanding, or other matters identified as spiritual. It occurs 26 times in the Greek New Testament, including several uses in Romans and 1 Corinthians. Its precise force depends on the noun or subject it describes in each sentence.

me: Verb, second Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means to suffer before or to suffer previously. It describes hardship that has already been endured before another event or point in view. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 2:2, and functions as a verb describing prior suffering. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is suffering experienced earlier.

This word means “before,” marking something as occurring earlier than another event, moment, or condition. It can point to what happened earlier in time or to a prior state in comparison with what follows. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times, showing a recurring way to establish sequence or priority without itself describing the event. Its exact force in a sentence depends on what earlier point the surrounding words identify.

This word means “wreath,” referring to a ring or circlet made from gathered material. It functions as a noun naming that object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 14:13. The word itself identifies a wreath, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain its particular use there. Its single occurrence makes it a specific term rather than a broadly repeated biblical expression.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Vocative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “be present with” or “to be present with.” It describes someone who is there alongside another person or group, emphasizing presence together rather than merely being nearby. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 25:24. Its basic sense is straightforward: people are present with others in the same situation. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular force of that presence in context.

This word means “quick” or “quickly,” describing an action that happens without delay. It commonly functions by adding urgency or speed to what someone does, rather than naming a person, object, or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, in five verses, from Matthew through Revelation. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea remains promptness and rapid action.

Tryphosa is a personal name identifying a person mentioned in the New Testament. It is not presented here as a word describing an action, quality, object, or belief; its function is to identify the person who bears the name. The name occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 16:12. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain anything about the person’s role or situation there.

This word means “healthy.” It describes a person or condition as sound, well, and free from illness or impairment. In the Greek New Testament, it is used in accounts involving bodily healing and restored health, while its broader sense can describe something sound or reliable. The word occurs 11 times across 11 verses, including several passages in John and accounts in Matthew and Mark. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This word means “to lower,” describing the act of bringing something or someone down from a higher position. It can refer to lowering a person, an object, or equipment, depending on the sentence. The word appears seven times in the Greek New Testament, including accounts involving lowering people or items and lowering equipment during travel. Its basic idea remains the same: something is moved downward. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being lowered and how the action serves the passage.

Arni is a personal name, rendered as “Arni.” It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it identifies a person by name. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once, in Luke 3:33. The available wording gives the name itself but does not provide further information about its meaning or the person who bore it. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on the surrounding genealogy and verse context.
